title: Vipassi's four sights
hookLine: the story of a past Buddha, Vipassi, who also saw the four sights

lines: AN OLD MAN BY THE ROAD.
cards: A prince rides out of the palace to the royal park. On the road his charioteer slows down. There's a man by the road, bent over, gray, leaning on a stick.
What's wrong with him? the prince asks. He's old, the charioteer says. Will I get old?
Everyone does, sir. The prince turns the chariot around and goes home, shaken. Most people know this scene as the young Siddhattha's.
But in the oldest detailed telling in the Pali canon, the prince in the chariot has a different name.

teach.b: The fourteenth Long Discourse, the Mahapadana, the great story, begins with monks chatting about past lives. The Buddha joins them and names six Buddhas before himself, going back ninety-one aeons to the first, Vipassi.
Then he tells Vipassi's life in full. Vipassi's father, King Bandhuma, hears a prediction that his son will either rule the world or leave it. So he surrounds him with pleasures.
Then, on four separate trips to the park, Vipassi sees an old man, then a sick man, then a dead man carried out with mourners.
Each time he turns back troubled, and each time his father adds more pleasures. On the fourth trip he sees a shaven-headed wanderer in a robe. What is he?
A man who has gone forth, sir, who lives kindly and harmlessly. Vipassi goes forth. Alone, he reflects: this world has fallen into trouble.
It's born, it ages, it dies. How does anyone escape? He traces the conditions back, link by link, and awakens.
Even his hesitation to teach is there, and a Brahma who asks him to. The sutta calls this kind of pattern dhammata, the way things are for every Buddha.

In the canon, the four sights are told in detail of Vipassi; later biographies tell the same scene of Gotama, the Buddha of our age. Why tell it this way? Because the point isn't one remarkable prince.
Whenever anyone looks clearly at aging, sickness and death, the same questions rise.

how: Theravada Buddhists honor seven Buddhas of the past, from Vipassi to Gotama, in chants such as the Atanatiya verses, and the four sights are retold in temples, festivals and art across the Buddhist world.

o: the charioteer who drove Prince Siddhattha
the king who filled his son's palace with pleasures
the first of seven Buddhas, who saw four sights

games.q: Vipassi's four sights: tap the pairs.
p: the first of seven Buddhas named

the Mahapadana Sutta tells them of Vipassi; later biographies tell them of Gotama.
Vipassi sees all four sights on a single trip
he makes four separate trips to the park, one sight each time.
DN 14 names six Buddhas before Gotama
Vipassi, Sikhi, Vessabhu, Kakusandha, Konagamana and Kassapa.

games.q: you're Prince Vipassi. on the road to the park you see a man bent with age, and learn that you will age too. what do you do?
o: carry on to the park and enjoy the day.
turn the chariot around and go home, troubled.
leave the palace that very hour.
games.why: he turns back troubled. his father answers by adding more pleasures. only after the fourth sight does Vipassi go forth.

practice: Let four faces come, one at a time: someone old you know, someone who is sick or was, someone who has died, and don't hurry past any of them.
Then a fourth: someone calm, who has made peace with some of this, and rest with that face. The questions Vipassi asked are yours to ask too, if you want them.

wordCard.voice: Vipassi, the first Buddha named in the Mahapadana Sutta, who saw age, sickness, death and a wanderer, a pattern later told of Gotama too. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali Vipassi: the name of the first Buddha named in DN 14. it is often heard as clear-seeing.

carryVoice: Your line: it happens again. People have stood exactly here before, asking the same questions. Day five hundred forty-three, done.
